theme: Abimelech’s treachery; the parable of the trees
readingInstruction: Read Judges 9:1-10:18. This is one of the darkest stretches of the book. Abimelech, Gideon’s son, murders his brothers and makes himself king. Read Jotham’s parable of the trees carefully. It is a sharp piece of political satire with a prophetic punch.
settingTheScene: Gideon has died, and Israel immediately returns to the Baals. Gideon’s son by a concubine, Abimelech, sees an opportunity. He persuades the leaders of Shechem to make him king, and then he murders seventy of his half-brothers on a single stone. One brother, Jotham, escapes, and from the top of Mount Gerizim he tells a parable. This chapter is a warning about what happens when power is seized by a man with no fear of God. It is also a sign that Israel is sliding from a nation of tribes toward a kingdom, but toward the wrong kind of king. The chapter closes with two more brief judges, Tola and Jair, and another round of oppression.
observation: Abimelech persuades his mother’s family to say to the leaders of Shechem, “Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you?” (9:2).
The leaders give him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith, and he hires worthless and reckless fellows (9:4).
He kills his seventy brothers “on one stone,” but Jotham, the youngest, hides (9:5).
Jotham’s parable: the olive tree, the fig tree, and the vine each refuse to rule, but the bramble agrees (9:7-15).
Jotham says, “let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem” (9:20).
“God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem” (9:23).
A woman drops a millstone on Abimelech’s head, and he asks his armor-bearer to kill him so that it will not be said a woman killed him (9:53-54).
“Thus God repaid the evil of Abimelech… and the evil of the men of Shechem God also repaid” (9:56-57).
interpretation:
Abimelech is a picture of the corruption of power. His name means “my father is king,” which says everything about his ambitions. He uses his family connections, the money from a pagan temple, and a gang of thugs to take control. The leaders of Shechem, who make him king, are complicit. They are willing to trade their loyalty to Jerubbaal’s family for a more convenient ruler, and they fund him from the treasury of Baal. The corruption is spiritual and political at once.

Jotham’s parable is the intellectual heart of the chapter. The trees go out to anoint a king. The olive tree, the fig tree, and the vine are all fruitful and useful, and each declines the offer, preferring to continue producing good things. Only the bramble, which produces nothing and is only good for burning, accepts. The sharp point is that those worth following have better things to do than seek power, and those who crave it are often the least fit. The bramble’s offer, “take refuge in my shade,” is absurd. A bramble offers no shade, and a fire may come from it.

The prophecy comes true. Within three years, God raises up strife between Abimelech and Shechem. The conspirators turn on each other, and both are destroyed. The narrator says plainly that God was repaying the evil done to the house of Gideon. The chapter is a case study in justice working itself out through the very sins people commit. Those who live by violence die by violence. Abimelech is killed by a millstone dropped from a tower by a woman, and his death is a bitter mockery of his pride.

The meaning is hardly cheerful, but it is clear. Human kingship without God is a bramble. It grasps, it burns, and it destroys. This sets the stage for a longer story. Israel will ask for a king in 1 Samuel, and the first, Saul, will be a disappointment. Only David will be a man after God’s own heart, and even he will fail. The longing for a true king runs through the whole Old Testament. The perfect king is the one who did not grasp at power but took the form of a servant. Philippians 2:5-8 describes the opposite of Abimelech. Christ, who had every right to rule, humbled himself and died. The true king is the true olive tree, the one who does not seek his own glory but gives himself.

Chapter 10 closes with a short note on two minor judges and then a statement of Israel’s apostasy: they serve the Baals, the Ashtaroth, and the gods of seven nations. God finally says, “I will save you no more,” but when they put away their foreign gods, “he became impatient over the misery of Israel.” His compassion overcomes his anger.
connection: Abimelech’s story echoes Cain’s murder of Abel (Genesis 4) and Absalom’s rebellion (2 Samuel 15). The parable of the trees is a fable like Nathan’s parable in 2 Samuel 12. The woman and the millstone appear again in 2 Samuel 11:21. Shechem was the place of the covenant in Joshua 24, and its fall here shows how far Israel has drifted. The true King contrasts with the bramble in Philippians 2:5-11 and Mark 10:42-45.
application:
Ask yourself what drives your ambitions. Are there areas where you are grasping for position, recognition, or control? Pray over them, and ask the Lord to give you the humility of Christ.

Consider whom you follow. The leaders of Shechem chose a bramble because he was convenient. Do you hold your leaders, in church, work, and society, to the standard of Scripture? Pray for those in authority over you.

Finally, take comfort that God sees. Abimelech’s crimes were hidden from earthly justice for a time, but not from God. Trust him to repay evil, and don’t take revenge into your own hands.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from grasping for power.
Ask him for the heart of the servant king.
Pray for leaders who fear him.
